migrations.whyTwo: The first migration shipped the retainer tables and CaseRetainerDraw, which records every movement of the allowance. It cannot record a STATE change, and CaseEvent could not be reused because CaseEvent.caseId is NOT NULL while a retainer legitimately exists before any case is linked to it. Fanning agreement events out to every linked case was rejected: a retainer with no links yet would then have no history at all, which is exactly the moment an owner most wants one. Requiring a linked case before activation would have made the gap unreachable rather than absent. So a second, strictly additive migration adds CaseRetainerEvent. It reuses CaseEventKind and CaseEventActor and therefore adds no vocabulary.
migrations.added: First: 9 tables, 11 enums, 14 CHECK constraints, 2 partial unique indexes, 6 triggers, 4 trigger functions. Second: 1 table, 0 enums, 1 trigger.

g3_1.oneNonAdditiveStatement: ALTER TYPE "CaseEventKind" ADD VALUE 'RETAINER' BEFORE 'NOTE'. Reusing 'NOTE' with a discriminator in the free-text `to` column was rejected, because a query for retainer history would become WHERE kind = 'NOTE' AND "to" LIKE 'RETAINER%' - the sort of encoding that quietly becomes a lie. CohortEventKind already carries a domain-specific RENEWAL.
g3_1.enumPosition: BEFORE 'NOTE' is load-bearing. Prisma emits a bare ADD VALUE, which Postgres appends at the END, leaving the database at (APPROVAL, NOTE, RETAINER) while schema.prisma reads (APPROVAL, RETAINER, NOTE). Postgres cannot reorder an enum afterwards, so the position is decided at insertion time or never. The build tool rewrites the statement with the substitution counted and asserted. Verified in the database and by a post-apply diff showing zero enum churn.
g3_1.rollbackOfAnEnum: Postgres cannot remove an enum value, so down.sql recreates the type in its original member order rather than pretending the rollback is a no-op, and refuses to run if any CaseEvent row already uses RETAINER. Verified: the rolled-back catalog is byte-identical, and the enum reads as its original nine labels.
g3_1.retainerShape: Workspace-scoped, linked to cases through CaseRetainerCaseLink rather than owning a single caseId. A retainer is an agreement with a client that work from several cases draws against; tying it to one case would have made 'renewal period' meaningless because you would be renewing per case rather than per agreement. The link table is a compound primary key with no surrogate id, the same shape as CaseTaskLink and CaseApprovalLink.
g3_1.snapshotAllowance: CaseRetainerPeriod snapshots its own included allowance rather than reading the agreement, so amending the agreement cannot rewrite what a closed period included.
g3_1.overageAllowed: used may exceed included, deliberately. Refusing a draw once an allowance is spent would misrepresent work that was actually done, and an owner who cannot see overage cannot bill for it. What IS constrained: used can never go negative; a draw must be denominated in the same basis as its period; a draw may only name a case the retainer covers; a draw may only belong to a period of its own retainer; a retainer and its linked cases must share a workspace. The last four are triggers, because a composite foreign key would express them and Prisma cannot describe one.
g3_1.selfVerifyingLedger: CaseRetainerDraw stores the signed delta AND the resulting used balance, the same shape as InventoryMovement. Replaying the deltas must reproduce the stored after-values, measured over a four-row ledger including a credit.
g3_1.accessLevelsBackwardCompatibility: This is the FIRST real content-visibility decision in the repository. Before it, any ACTIVE or COMPLETED enrolment returned every module and every lesson, and CourseLesson.isFree was written by importers and enforced by nothing. A lesson with no CourseLessonAccess row is unrestricted; no existing lesson has one; so nothing changes for anybody and there is no backfill to get wrong. Measured, not asserted, on a seeded three-tier course.
g3_1.grantIdentity: CourseAccessGrant is keyed on enrollmentId UNIQUE - one grant per enrolment - because the enrolment is already the learner-to-course record the content reader resolves. That makes the grant idempotent by identity: asking twice finds the same row, so it needs no idempotency key. CourseAccessChange does carry one.
g3_1.tenancy: profileId throughout, never workspaceId, asserted per table. Matches the cohort domain exactly.

g3_2.twoStateMachinesEach: Retainers: the AGREEMENT is what the client signed, the PERIOD is one window inside it. Access: the ENTITLEMENT is what a learner holds, the CHANGE is one requested move. Separating them is what lets a period close without ending an agreement, and an upgrade be approved without yet being true.
g3_2.reversibleVsTerminal: PAUSED is reversible, CANCELLED and EXPIRED are terminal - reviving a cancelled agreement would make the draw ledger ambiguous about which engagement a draw belonged to. SUSPENDED is reversible, REVOKED is not, for the same reason about access history.
g3_2.threeEndings: CLOSED, RENEWED and LAPSED are three different period endings and only LAPSED is a problem to report. RENEWED is the only one that creates the next period, and it does so in the same transaction, so a renewal cannot half-happen.
g3_2.rollover: Measured: 100000 included + 70000 unused carried forward = 170000 on the next period, only when the agreement allows it.
g3_2.unlinkRefused: A case that has drawn cannot be unlinked, because the ledger rows name that case and removing the link would leave history referring to a coverage the records now deny.
g3_2.concurrency: MEASURED with genuinely parallel operations: two draws fired at one open period BOTH land, and their after-balances chain correctly. This is the OPPOSITE of the inventory case where exactly one writer wins - consumption is additive, so a lost writer would silently forget real work. The period row is locked FOR UPDATE first so the two serialise.
g3_2.twoPrincipals: CourseAccessService is the owner surface and composes CohortContext. LearnerAccessService takes NO workspaceId at all: a learner is a Member with a cookie session, not a Clerk user with a workspace membership, and letting a learner name a workspace would hand them a probe.
g3_2.oneVisibilityComputation: The visibility rule lives in ONE function that both services call, so the owner console and the learner surface cannot disagree. Asserted by comparing their outputs directly.
g3_2.suspensionIsNotDowngrade: A SUSPENDED or EXPIRED grant falls back to the unruled lessons, NOT to the lowest tier. Measured.
g3_2.expiryComputed: A grant past its expiry stops entitling immediately while its state remains ACTIVE. There is no sweep and no cached entitlement column - the cohort schema harness forbids cached progress tables by name.
g3_2.directionDerived: UPGRADE versus DOWNGRADE is derived by comparing ranks, so a downgrade cannot be presented as an upgrade.
g3_2.approveIsNotApply: Requesting changes nothing, approving changes nothing, only applying moves the entitlement. All three measured separately. Applying is refused if the entitlement moved since approval, so an approval cannot overwrite a tier it was never agreed against.
g3_2.reversible: Removing a lesson rule restores the original behaviour, so the feature can be backed out with no data migration.
g3_2.noPaymentExecution: Measured on both sides. The retainer's full billing lifecycle - DRAFT, ISSUED against a real CaseInvoice, PAID - leaves the Payment row count unmoved. A complete course upgrade with an invoice reference does the same. Every change event stores paymentExecuted: false so the history cannot be read as a charge.
g3_2.nonEnumeration: Compared byte for byte on serialized envelopes, not by status code. Learner path: unknown course, another owner's course, a stranger's request and a cancelled enrolment are all identical. Owner path: a foreign retainer and a nonexistent one are identical.
g3_2.fixtureBugFoundByConstraints: The expiry test initially set expiresAt in the past on a grant whose grantedAt was now, which CourseAccessGrant_expiry_after_grant correctly refused. The test now moves both timestamps and additionally asserts the invalid combination is refused - the constraint found the bug, not review.

tasks.notAFullEngine: fieldJobs:inspection is deliberately NOT built and stays declared planned with evidence 'none'. Asset checks, parts, completion notes and invoice handoff are absent on purpose. The commit messages, the migration header, the capability description and the ledger all say so, so three available-sounding capabilities cannot imply a finished engine.

reuse.technician: A field technician IS an AppointmentResource with kind STAFF. That table is already profile-scoped, already optionally tied to a Location, already carries capacity and isActive, and is already what ServiceOffering rows are made eligible for. A separate Technician table would have been a second answer to 'who can do this work', and the two would have drifted the first time somebody was added to one and not the other.
reuse.consequence: Tenancy is therefore profileId, bridged from Workspace.profileId. That is forced rather than chosen: sharing AppointmentResource means sharing its scope. The harness asserts no fieldJobs table has a workspaceId.
reuse.byReferenceNotExtension: AppointmentResource, ServiceOffering and Location are asserted to have gained no columns - AppointmentResource is pinned at exactly 9 columns. Reuse is by foreign key, not by extension. The runtime harness additionally asserts the technician rows are the same AppointmentResource rows (count moves by exactly the 5 seeded) and that no Booking row was created.
reuse.siteIsNotALocation: Location models the owner's own premises and is read by the reservation, appointment and inventory engines. Creating Location rows for customer addresses would pollute it, so FieldJob.siteAddress is required free text and originLocationId is only the depot the job is dispatched FROM.
reuse.requestIsNotAJob: FieldJobRequest is separate from FieldJob for the same reason CaseIntake is separate from CaseProject: a declined request must remain a record, and a job that exists must mean somebody committed to it. Collapsing them would make 'how many jobs do we have' unanswerable. One request converts to at most one job, enforced by UNIQUE on FieldJob.requestId.

tasks.whatDispatchDoesNotDo: No route is optimised, no distance or travel time is computed, no map provider is called, and no technician is notified by email, SMS or push. The schema harness asserts there is no routeId, routeOrder, distanceMeters, travelMinutes, latitude, longitude, notifiedAt, smsSentAt, emailSentAt, pushSentAt or providerMessageId column anywhere in the four tables, and that no Route, Inspection, Part, Asset, Invoice or Notification table exists. The runtime harness replaces global fetch with a counting blocker and asserts zero calls, and asserts every assignment event records notified: false.
tasks.sideConditions: The design work is in the side conditions on job transitions, each exported as a named list in lifecycle.ts rather than buried in an if. MEASURED: a job with no visit window cannot be scheduled or dispatched; a job cannot be dispatched without an accountable LEAD and a helper alone is not enough; work cannot start until a technician is ON_SITE; a job is not complete while any card is still ASSIGNED, ACCEPTED, EN_ROUTE or ON_SITE, and the refusal names how many; cancelling a job, declining a card and releasing a card all need a reason, and whitespace does not count.
tasks.assignmentIsARequest: ASSIGNED cannot jump to EN_ROUTE - a technician has to answer first. Recording only ASSIGNED would make a silent refusal look like agreement. ACCEPTED and DECLINED both exist for that reason, and a technician who declined can be assigned again because both partial unique indexes exclude DECLINED and RELEASED, so the declined row survives.
tasks.directionality: SCHEDULED can return to DRAFT, because un-scheduling is normal when a customer moves. DISPATCHED cannot return to SCHEDULED, because a technician has already been told. An IN_PROGRESS job can still be CANCELLED, because work does get abandoned. A COMPLETED job is terminal and cannot be cancelled.
tasks.guarantees: 6 CHECK constraints: non-negative estimates on both tables; a job's schedule is both timestamps or neither; the end must be after the start; a DECLINED card must carry a non-blank reason; so must a RELEASED one. 2 partial unique indexes: one active LEAD per job, and one active assignment per technician per job. 1 trigger enforcing that a job and its technician share a profile - the same shape as the four G3 guards, a rule a composite foreign key would express if Prisma could describe one. 1 append-only trigger on FieldJobEvent, the tenth ledger in this database.

Post-apply drift: 0 of everything except the five pre-existing profileId DROP CONSTRAINT statements, ninth wave running. Relation verifier: 4 models added, 0 renamed, 0 dropped.

api.routes: 10 routes: field-job-requests (GET/POST), [requestId] (PATCH status), [requestId]/quote (PATCH), [requestId]/convert (POST), field-jobs (GET with a status filter, POST), [jobId] (GET/PATCH), [jobId]/schedule (PATCH), [jobId]/assignments (GET/POST), [jobId]/assignments/[assignmentId] (PATCH), [jobId]/timeline (GET).
api.conversionIsItsOwnRoute: Conversion is a POST to its own route rather than a status PATCH, because a request becomes CONVERTED by a job existing. The status route refuses CONVERTED with a 409 that says so, so there is exactly one way to do it and the wrong way explains itself.
api.theActorBoundary: THE ONE THING THIS SURFACE DOES DIFFERENTLY. Cases and cohorts derive a fixed STAFF actor and offer no way to name yourself. Field jobs genuinely have two actors: an office staffer moving a job card on a technician's behalf is a different fact from the technician moving it, and a history that cannot tell them apart is worth less. So a write may declare actorType: 'TECHNICIAN'. That makes the actor an INPUT, which is exactly what an audit trail must not over-trust, so the boundary is narrow and proven: STAFF and TECHNICIAN accepted, CUSTOMER and SYSTEM refused with 400, actorId never taken from the caller whatever is sent. When stock does move it goes through InventoryService.applyMovement as an ADJUSTMENT with a NEGATIVE quantity, not a CONSUME. That is the inventory engine's own rule: CONSUME only arises from settling a reservation, and a part off a van has no hold behind it, so accepting CONSUME would move the reserved balance with nothing backing it.

Part ordering is deliberate. The part row is written FIRST so the database's boundary trigger validates tenant, depot and existence before any stock moves; then the movement is applied with an idempotency key DERIVED FROM THE PART ID; then the movement id is stored. A crash mid-way leaves a visible part with no movement - recorded, stock not moved - rather than stock that vanished with nothing pointing at it, and a retry with the same key finishes the job without deducting twice.

The timeline filters by subject IDENTITY (the inspection id plus its item and part ids), not by subjectType alone, because item events carry the item's id and a subjectType-only filter would return every inspection's lines on the same job.

schema.notCreated: no FAILED state, no REFUSED event kind, no Blueprint registry table, no FK on blueprintId, and none of the 13 forbidden tables

designDecisions: NO WORKFLOW TEMPLATE TABLE. blueprint.id encodes the version and the registry RETAINS deprecated entries, so pinning an id is already immutable. Copying the declarations would create a second source of truth able to disagree with the first, and reconciling them would become somebody's permanent job.

NO SURFACE OR TERMINOLOGY TABLE. Surfaces already live per profile as JSON on Profile.personalityConfig. An unscoped Terminology table is on the design's forbidden list; the resolved pack is frozen into configJson on a workspace-scoped row, so it is scoped by construction.

INSTALL DOES NOT WRITE Profile.personalityConfig, so it grants nothing. The reason is structural, not cautious: surfaces are per PROFILE, an installation is per WORKSPACE, and a user reaches many workspaces through Membership (keyed by userId). Applying workspace-scoped intent to a profile-scoped store would change what that user sees in workspaces the install said nothing about.

NO FAILED STATE AND NO REFUSED EVENT. A refusal row is a partial write, and the zero-partial-rows proof would need an exception carved out of it. An assertion with an exception is the kind that stops noticing.
NO METHOD TO EDIT A CONFIG. Editing a frozen record of what was agreed to is how an audit trail stops being one. A configuration change is an upgrade, and upgrades supersede.
config is FROZEN at install time and drift is REPORTED rather than silently corrected, because the useful question is 'what did this workspace agree to', not 'what would we resolve today'.

Install asks for workspace.update rather than profile.update. MANAGER holds profile.update, and a manager being able to change what the business IS would be a silent permission expansion achieved by picking the permission that happened to be there. No new permission KEY was added, because adding one to PERMISSION_KEYS extends the OWNER and ADMIN closures automatically and forces a decision about every other role.
lessons: A BEFORE DELETE TRIGGER OUTRANKS A CASCADE. onDelete: Cascade plus an append-only ledger means a workspace with installation history can never be deleted - the cascaded DELETE still fires the trigger. This is consistent with ActivityEvent and CopilotAuditEvent, which have made Contact and workspace deletion conditional the same way for far longer, but it is a real consequence of choosing append-only and the schema harness now asserts BOTH directions: cascade works with no history, and is refused once there is history. The first version asserted only the no-history case and so advertised a deletion path that does not exist in practice.

TRIGGER ORDER CAN MAKE A CHECK CONSTRAINT UNREACHABLE. On INSERT the supersession trigger fires before the no_self_supersession CHECK and refuses first, because the row being pointed at does not exist yet. An assertion that only tried INSERT would have claimed to test a constraint it never reached. Both statements are now asserted and the CHECK is proven reachable by UPDATE, which is the one that can reach it.

IN POSTGRES ANY SQL ERROR ABORTS THE ENCLOSING TRANSACTION. A harness that shares one outer transaction across its assertions cannot contain a trigger refusal and then continue - every later assertion fails with 25P02 while appearing to be about whatever it was named after. Database-level refusals belong in a harness that gives each one its own transaction.

RESIDUE IN A SHARED DATABASE IS A DEFECT, NOT AN INCONVENIENCE. The atomicity proof needs the real transaction, and proving the idempotency key survived by performing a real retry wrote a PERMANENT ledger line. One surviving profile-with-workspace made check-schema-invariants.ts fail three files away, because it projects every Profile into a Workspace and Workspace.profileId is UNIQUE.
